config.prompt: Which quantities survive every stretching and bending (no tearing)?
config.why: Topology keeps what deformation cannot change; distance, angle and area are all destroyed by stretching.

config.root: You want to define a topological space. What is the minimal specification?

choices.label: A set plus a family of open sets satisfying the axioms
choices.feedback: Yes — nearness is specified by open sets, with no distance required.

choices.label: A set plus a distance function
choices.feedback: That defines a metric space, a special case; topology is more general.

choices.label: A set plus a list of its points
choices.feedback: A bare set has no nearness structure at all.

right.text: A set with a declared family of open sets — the economy is the point, because surfaces, function spaces and solution spaces all become instances of one structure.

metric.text: Metric spaces are examples, but topology deliberately drops the distance.

choices.label: What replaces distance?
choices.feedback: The open sets themselves encode nearness.

points.text: Without open sets there is no notion of nearness or continuity.

choices.label: So what must be added?
choices.feedback: A declared family of open sets.

config.why: A topological space is a set plus open sets; metric spaces are the special case where open balls come from a distance.

config.prompt: Find the line where the Brouwer contradiction is misstated:
lines: Suppose a continuous map of the disk to itself has no fixed point.
Then every point x moves, so draw the ray from f(x) through x to the boundary.
This defines a continuous retraction of the disk onto its boundary circle.
But the boundary circle admits no such retraction, by a winding-number argument.
Therefore some point must move — the fixed point exists.
config.correction: The contradiction forces the assumption to fail: some point does not move — that is the fixed point.
config.why: Existence is forced by the impossibility of a disk retraction; no coordinates are constructed.

config.prompt: Two ways convergence survives without a ruler — drag the divider:

before.label: sequences
before.text: in a metric space, distances shrink to zero — enough to detect the topology

after.label: nets and filters
after.text: in a general topological space, sequences can be too poor; convergence is indexed by open sets

config.why: Compactness restores power: compact metric spaces are sequentially compact, and open covers turn local control into global truth.

config.prompt: In the Königsberg bridge problem, how many landmasses had an odd number of bridge-ends?
config.why: All four had odd degree, so an Euler walk crossing every bridge once is impossible — an even degree at every vertex is required for a closed walk.
config.context: Euler solved it in 1736 without distances, angles or a map

activities.caption: continuous bijection versus homeomorphism — drag the divider
activities.name: toHomeoCompare

config.prompt: Same shape or not? — drag the divider:

before.label: continuous bijection
before.text: the half-open interval wraps once round the circle: continuous forwards, but the inverse tears at the join

after.label: homeomorphism
after.text: a bijection whose inverse is also continuous — the extra clause rules out the tear

config.why: The wrapped-interval map is the standard counterexample; homeomorphism's extra clause is doing real work.

activities.anchor: Curve sketching (E2.11) assumes something so obvious
activities.caption: compute a winding number
activities.name: toWindingOrder

config.prompt: Compute a winding number — put the steps in order:
items: Walk once around a closed loop
Total the turning angle along the way
The total comes to 360° times an integer
For a simple loop that integer is 1
The integer cannot change under deformation
config.why: The winding number is the computable invariant behind fixed-point theorems, residues and ray-casting inside-a-polygon tests.
